lessons.title: Estimating and Costing
lessons.body: Estimating and costing is how you figure out what to charge for a steel fabrication job so you make a profit and don't go broke. Start by measuring the job. For a simple gate, measure width, height, and count bars. If you use 20mm square tubing, each meter weighs about 1.2 kg. Steel costs around $1.20 per kg in many African cities. So a 5-meter gate frame using 12 meters of tubing needs 14.4 kg, costing about $17. Add hinges, paint, and consumables like welding rods and grinding discs. A 5kg box of rods costs $8 and you might use half. Paint: 1 liter covers 5 square meters and costs $6. A gate has about 3 square meters of surface, so $4 of paint. Now labor: if you pay a helper $10 per day and the job takes 2 days, that's $20. Add your own time at $15 per day for 2 days = $30. Overhead: electricity for welder, rent, wear on tools. Estimate 10% of material and labor. Total material: $17 + $4 + $4 = $25. Labor: $50. Overhead: $7.50. Total cost: $82.50. Now add profit. A 30% markup gives $107.25. Round to $110. Always add 10% contingency for mistakes or price changes. Keep a notebook of all costs per job. After the job, compare actual to estimate. If you spent more on grinding discs, adjust next time. In Africa, steel prices change often due to imports. Call your supplier for current prices before quoting. Never quote from memory. Use a simple calculator and write everything down. For bigger jobs like staircases, break into sections: stringers, treads, handrails. Estimate each separately. Remember transport: hiring a truck to deliver the gate might cost $20. Include that. If you forget, you lose profit. Also, charge for design time if you draw plans. A good estimate wins the job and keeps you in business.

lessons.title: Production Planning and Scheduling
lessons.body: Production planning means deciding what work to do, in what order, and when, so you meet deadlines without chaos. Start with a job list. Write each project, its deadline, and how many hours it needs. For example, you have three jobs: a window frame (4 hours), a door (8 hours), and a trailer repair (12 hours). You have two workers and one welder. You work 8 hours a day, 5 days a week. Total hours needed: 24. With two workers, you have 16 hours per day. So you can finish in 2 days if no delays. But you must schedule tasks that need the welder first, because only one person can weld at a time. Make a simple chart: Monday morning: cut all steel for all jobs. Monday afternoon: weld window frame. Tuesday morning: weld door. Tuesday afternoon: start trailer. Wednesday: finish trailer and paint everything. This is a Gantt chart in your notebook. Always plan for 20% extra time for delays: power cuts, material shortages, sick workers. In Africa, power cuts are common. If you have a generator, schedule welding during likely power cuts. If not, do cutting and grinding when power is out. Keep a whiteboard in the shop with each job and its status: not started, in progress, done. Update it daily. Order materials at least 3 days before you need them. Steel suppliers may take time. For a big job like a roof truss, break into stages: cutting, welding, drilling, painting, delivery. Assign each stage a day. Tell the customer a realistic completion date, not an optimistic one. If you promise Friday and deliver Monday, you lose trust. Use a calendar and mark deadlines in red. Check progress every morning for 5 minutes with your team. Ask: what did you finish yesterday? What will you finish today? What do you need? This keeps everyone focused. If a job runs late, decide whether to work overtime or move another job. Never sacrifice safety for speed. A planned shop is a profitable shop.

lessons.title: Inventory and Material Management
lessons.body: Inventory and material management is about knowing what steel, tools, and consumables you have, where they are, and when to reorder. Without this, you waste money buying duplicates or lose jobs because you ran out of welding rods. Start by organizing your shop into zones: steel rack, tool cabinet, consumables shelf, and scrap bin. Label everything. Use a notebook or a simple spreadsheet on your phone. For each item, record: description, size, quantity, minimum stock level, and supplier. For example: 20mm square tubing, 6-meter lengths, 10 pieces, minimum 4 pieces. When you take a piece, write it down. When you buy, add it. Do a physical count every Friday afternoon. This takes 30 minutes but saves hours. Set reorder points. If you use 2 pieces of tubing per week, and delivery takes 1 week, keep at least 4 pieces as minimum. When stock hits 4, order 10 more. For consumables like grinding discs, welding rods, and paint, keep a minimum of one week's usage. A 5kg box of 3.2mm rods lasts about 20 hours of welding. If you weld 4 hours a day, that's 5 days. So keep 2 boxes. Store steel off the ground on wooden pallets to prevent rust. Cover with a tarp in rainy season. Keep paint and thinners in a locked metal cabinet away from welding sparks. Tools: keep grinders, drills, and clamps in a cabinet. Assign one person to be tool keeper. They sign tools out and in. If a tool breaks, tag it and tell the owner. Never leave tools on the floor. Scrap: keep all offcuts longer than 30cm in a bin. You will use them for small jobs like brackets. Sell truly unusable scrap to a recycler. In Africa, theft can be a problem. Lock your shop at night. Keep a record of who has keys. A well-managed shop never stops work because of missing materials.

lessons.title: Shop Safety and OSHA Regulations
lessons.body: Shop safety is not optional. In steel fabrication, you face burns, cuts, eye injuries, and electric shock. OSHA (Occupational Safety and Health Administration) sets rules that many countries adopt. Even if your country doesn't enforce them, follow them to stay alive and productive. First, personal protective equipment (PPE). Always wear safety glasses when grinding, cutting, or chipping. A grinding disc can shatter and blind you. Wear a welding helmet with at least shade 10 for arc welding. Wear leather gloves when handling steel. Wear steel-toe boots. Wear ear plugs when grinding for long periods. Wear a respirator when painting or welding galvanized steel (which releases toxic zinc fumes). Second, fire safety. Keep a fire extinguisher (dry chemical, ABC type) within 10 meters of welding. Never weld near paint, thinners, or gas cylinders. Keep a bucket of sand or water for small fires. Third, electrical safety. Inspect welder cables for cracks. Never weld in wet conditions. Use a ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) if possible. Turn off welder when changing electrodes. Fourth, machine safety. Use guards on grinders. Never remove the guard. Clamp workpieces securely. Keep hands away from the blade. Fifth, housekeeping. Keep floors dry and free of scrap. Trip hazards cause falls. Store gas cylinders upright and chained. Sixth, ventilation. Weld in a well-ventilated area or use a fume extractor. Manganese fumes cause Parkinson's-like symptoms. Seventh, training. Every worker must know where the first aid kit is and how to use it. Have a first aid kit with burn gel, bandages, and eye wash. Eighth, emergency plan. Know the nearest clinic and have a phone number. In Africa, many shops lack formal OSHA enforcement, but you can self-regulate. Post safety rules on the wall. Hold a 5-minute safety talk every Monday. Lead by example: wear your PPE. If you see unsafe act, stop it. A safe shop has fewer accidents, less downtime, and better morale.

lessons.title: Team Leadership and Communication
lessons.body: Team leadership and communication is how you get your workers to do quality work on time without fighting. In a small African shop, you might have 2 to 10 workers. You are the boss, but you also work alongside them. Respect is key. Start each day with a 10-minute meeting. Stand in a circle. Ask each person what they will do today. Listen. Then assign tasks clearly: 'John, you cut all the 40mm tubing for the gate. Mary, you weld the frame. I will grind and paint.' Give deadlines: 'Finish cutting by 11am.' Check progress at lunch. If someone is slow, ask why. Maybe the blade is dull. Fix the problem, don't just shout. Communicate in the language everyone understands. If you have workers from different tribes, use the common language (English, French, Swahili, etc.). Avoid sarcasm. Give feedback privately if it's negative. Praise publicly. When a worker does good work, say 'Thank you, that weld is clean.' A simple thank you costs nothing and builds loyalty. Pay wages on time. If you delay pay, workers steal or leave. If you can't pay, tell them early and agree on a plan. Train your team. Show a new worker how to hold a grinder safely. Let them practice on scrap. Don't just throw them into a job. Cross-train: teach everyone to weld, cut, and paint. Then if one person is sick, work continues. Handle conflicts quickly. If two workers argue, separate them and talk to each one alone. Find a solution. Never take sides without facts. Keep a notebook of worker skills and attendance. Reward good attendance with a small bonus or lunch. In Africa, many workers support extended families. A small bonus means a lot. Lead by example: be on time, wear PPE, clean up. If you work hard, they will too. A good team makes your shop profitable and your life easier.

lessons.title: Capstone Fabrication Project
lessons.body: The capstone project brings together everything you learned in this module. You will plan, estimate, schedule, manage materials, work safely, and lead a team to build a real steel product. Choose a project that is useful and sellable. A good choice is a double gate for a compound, a staircase for a two-story house, or a set of window frames for a small shop. For this example, we build a 3-meter wide double gate. Step 1: Estimate. Measure opening: 3m wide, 1.8m high. Use 40mm square tubing for frame, 20mm for bars. Calculate steel: frame needs 2 verticals (1.8m each) + 3 horizontals (1.5m each) = 3.6 + 4.5 = 8.1m of 40mm. Bars: 10 vertical bars per leaf, 1.5m each, 2 leaves = 30m of 20mm. Weight: 40mm is 2.4kg/m, so 19.4kg. 20mm is 1.2kg/m, so 36kg. Total 55.4kg. At $1.20/kg = $66.50. Hinges, latch, paint: $20. Labor: 2 workers x 3 days x $10 = $60. Overhead 10% = $14.65. Total cost = $161.15. Add 30% profit = $209.50. Quote $210. Step 2: Plan. Day 1: cut all steel. Day 2: weld frames. Day 3: weld bars, grind, paint. Day 4: install. Step 3: Inventory. Check you have 20kg of 40mm, 40kg of 20mm, 2 boxes of rods, 5 grinding discs, 1 liter paint, 2 hinges, 1 latch. Order missing items. Step 4: Safety. Wear PPE. Set up fire extinguisher. Ensure ventilation. Step 5: Team. Assign tasks: Worker A cuts, Worker B welds, you grind and paint. Hold morning meetings. Step 6: Build. Follow your drawing. Measure twice, cut once. Weld clean. Grind smooth. Paint two coats. Step 7: Install. Dig post holes, set posts in concrete, hang gates. Check swing. Step 8: Review. Compare actual cost to estimate. Note what went wrong. This project proves you can run a fabrication job from start to finish.

quiz.q: What is the first step in estimating a steel fabrication job?
quiz.explanation: You must measure the job to know how much material and labor it will require.

quiz.q: If 20mm square tubing weighs 1.2 kg per meter, how much does 12 meters weigh?
quiz.explanation: 12 meters multiplied by 1.2 kg/m equals 14.4 kg.

quiz.q: Why should you add a 10% contingency to your estimate?
options: A) To cover mistakes or price changes
quiz.explanation: A contingency covers unexpected costs like material price increases or errors.

quiz.q: What should you do after finishing a job regarding your estimate?
options: B) Compare actual costs to estimate
C) Double the price next time
quiz.explanation: Comparing actual to estimated costs helps you improve future estimates.

quiz.q: In production planning, what is a Gantt chart used for?
quiz.explanation: A Gantt chart visually shows tasks scheduled over time.

quiz.q: Why should you plan for 20% extra time in a schedule?
options: A) To allow for delays like power cuts
quiz.explanation: Unforeseen delays such as power cuts or material shortages are common.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for ordering materials?
options: A) Order the same day you need them
B) Order at least 3 days before needed
D) Order after the job is done
quiz.explanation: Ordering early ensures materials arrive before work starts.

quiz.q: What should you do every morning with your team?
options: D) Only talk to the supervisor
quiz.explanation: A short daily check keeps everyone focused and informed.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a minimum stock level?
options: A) To know when to reorder
quiz.explanation: When stock hits the minimum, you reorder to avoid running out.

quiz.q: How often should you do a physical inventory count?
quiz.explanation: Weekly counts catch discrepancies early and keep records accurate.

quiz.q: Why should steel be stored off the ground?
quiz.explanation: Ground moisture causes rust; pallets or racks keep steel dry.

quiz.q: Where should paint and thinners be stored?
options: B) In a locked metal cabinet
quiz.explanation: Flammable liquids must be kept away from sparks and locked up.

quiz.q: What does PPE stand for?
quiz.explanation: PPE is the gear you wear to protect yourself from hazards.

quiz.q: What shade of welding helmet lens is recommended for arc welding?
quiz.explanation: Shade 10 or higher protects eyes from arc flash.

quiz.q: Why is ventilation important when welding galvanized steel?
options: A) It releases toxic zinc fumes
quiz.explanation: Galvanized steel produces zinc oxide fumes that are harmful if inhaled.

quiz.q: What type of fire extinguisher is recommended for welding areas?
quiz.explanation: ABC dry chemical extinguishers handle electrical, flammable liquid, and ordinary fires.

quiz.q: What should you do before changing a welding electrode?
quiz.explanation: Turning off the welder prevents electric shock.

quiz.q: What is a good housekeeping practice in a shop?
options: A) Keep floors dry and free of scrap
quiz.explanation: Clean floors prevent slips, trips, and falls.

quiz.q: How often should you hold a safety talk with your team?
quiz.explanation: Weekly safety talks reinforce safe habits.

quiz.q: What is the best way to give negative feedback to a worker?
quiz.explanation: Private feedback respects the worker and avoids resentment.

quiz.q: Why is cross-training workers beneficial?
options: A) Work continues if someone is absent
D) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Cross-trained workers can cover for each other, keeping production going.

quiz.q: What should you do if you cannot pay wages on time?
options: A) Tell workers early and agree on a plan
quiz.explanation: Honest communication maintains trust and loyalty.

quiz.q: How can you reward good attendance?
quiz.explanation: Small rewards motivate workers and show appreciation.

quiz.q: What is a key leadership behavior?
quiz.explanation: Leading by example sets the standard for the team.

quiz.q: In the capstone project, what is the first step?
quiz.explanation: Estimating determines cost and guides the whole project.

quiz.q: For the double gate example, what is the total steel weight?
quiz.explanation: 19.4 kg of 40mm plus 36 kg of 20mm equals 55.4 kg.

quiz.q: What is the total cost before profit in the gate example?
quiz.explanation: Material $86.50, labor $60, overhead $14.65 sum to $161.15.

quiz.q: What should you do after completing the capstone project?
options: A) Review actual vs estimated cost
quiz.explanation: Reviewing helps you learn and improve for next time.

quiz.q: Why is measuring twice and cutting once important?
quiz.explanation: Double-checking measurements prevents costly cutting errors.

quiz.q: What is a key part of installing a gate?
quiz.explanation: Posts must be securely set in concrete for stability.
